previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, and recent SVC repair presented with fever, chills, and right-sided chest pain. She was found to have a superficial thrombus in the right basilic vein and evidence of right upper lobe pneumonia on imaging. She was treated with IV antibiotics, which were later transitioned to oral levofloxacin, and continued on fondaparinux for HIT. Her fever resolved within 48 hours, and she improved clinically. A PICC line could not be placed due to extensive venous occlusive disease. She was discharged home in stable condition with a plan for outpatient antibiotic completion and follow-up.

s/p multiple bowel resections and rectovaginal fistula, 
extensive venous thromboses, depression, anxiety, PTSD, and SVC 
syndrome s/p SVC reconstruction with bovine pericardial patch 
and SVC endarterectomy on ___, who presents with bloody 
diarrhea, fever, nausea, vomiting.

1) Crohn's Flare:  The patient presented with bloody diarrhea 
and right lower quadrant pain.  Given her history leading 
diagnosis was a Crohn's flare.  Though she has not previously 
had bleeding with these flares this could have been precipitated 
by currently anticoagulation.  She was seen by GI and started on 
ciprofloxacin and metronidazole (as she has been intolerant of 
prednisone and most other treatments).  She received 
anti-emetics and analgesics for her nausea and pain 
respectively.  Per GI reccs cultures were done for common 
diarrhea pathogens and they were negative (including C diff 
negative).  CRP was elevated, also suggestive of Crohn's flare, 
though this could have also been up from her recent surgery.  
KUB showed no obstructive pattern and patient continued to have 
bowel movements.  Nausea was felt more likely due to 
inflammation from active Crohns.  Gastroenterology thought 
further imaging to rule out partial obstruction and pinpoint an 
area of colitis could be useful given the patient's history, but 
this was not able to be obtained due to persistent issues with 
access.  Despite some blood in stools her anemia remained 
stable.  She was discharged on ciprofloxacin and metronidazole 
to follow up with her outpatient providers. 

2) Acute on chronic abdominal pain/nausea: The patient was 
managed on IV hydromorphone as well as IV diazepam, IV 
diphenhydramine, and promethazine in house.  These were 
initially dripped but the patient was very disatisfied with this 
method feeling it led to failure of her IVs due to the pump and 
was less effective.  On hospital day 2 the acute pain team was 
consulted and recommended PCA management but this was 
discontinued as IV access was lost.  She was switched to PO 
hydromorphone and benzodiazepine as well as rectal phenergan 
prior to discharge and tolerated these. 

3) ? Pneumonia: The patient had been diagnosed with pneumonia 
during a recent hospitalization with vascular surgery.  She was 
given a two week course of levofloxacin.  She presented 
approximately eight days into this course, which should have 
been more than adequate coverage.  Her continued ciprofloxacin 
was considered a reasonable substitute for the last six days.  

4) Access: The patient has very poor IV access, which is well 
known.  She has had 4+ hour attempts by ___ to place femoral 
lines, which have ultimately been unsuccessful.  Therefore, when 
IV access was lost on hospital day 2 and there were no further 
possible IV's or EJ's appreciated the patient and her husband 
reasonably were quite doubtful new IV access could be obtained 
in a short time.  Therefore, given this and the risks associated 
with further central access attempts they elected in discussion 
with the team to transition to PO or PR formulations of meds.  
It was recommended she stay overnight to make sure she was 
tolerating these formulations but given the extreme stress and 
anxiety prompted by hospitalization in the patient she and her 
husband after discussion with the attending MD elected to return 
home after a much shorter oral trial of medications.  

5) s/p SVC repair/HIT: She was continued on her home 
___.  

6) Hypothyroidism: Continued levothyroxine.  
  
7) Depression/Anxiety: Continued citalopram & oxazepam.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  Fever.

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph from ___. Chest CTA from ___.

PA AND LATERAL VIEWS OF THE CHEST:  The patient is status post median
sternotomy.  The cardiac, mediastinal and hilar contours are unchanged, with
widening of the right paratracheal stripe due to known fluid collection and
mediastinal lymphadenopathy.  There is continued volume loss within the right
upper lobe with bronchiectasis and interstitial opacities, not significantly
changed when compared to the prior CTA from ___ or the prior
radiograph.  The left lung remains clear.  Pulmonary vascularity is not
engorged.  Trace left pleural effusion is unchanged.  No pneumothorax is
present.  Several clips are again noted projecting over the right upper chest.
Cylindrical opacity projecting over the left upper lobe is unchanged.  No
acute osseous abnormalities are seen.  A nasogastric tube tip terminates
within the stomach, but the side port is likely above the gastroesophageal
junction and should be advanced.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Unchanged volume loss with bronchiectasis and interstitial markings in the
right upper lobe.

2.  Nasogastric tube tip terminates in the stomach, however the side port is
likely above the gastroesophageal junction and should be advanced.

3.  Persistently widened right paratracheal stripe corresponding to known
fluid collection and lymphadenopathy as seen on prior CT.

INDICATION:  Abdominal pain and history of small-bowel obstruction.

COMPARISON:  ___.

UPRIGHT AND SUPINE AP VIEWS OF THE ABDOMEN:  Nasogastric tube tip is seen
within the stomach, however, the side port likely lies above the
gastroesophageal junction.  Nonspecific bowel gas pattern is present with
gaseous distention centrally of a loop of bowel, which may represent large
bowel.  Few scattered air-fluid levels are noted on the upright view.  There
is no free intraperitoneal air.  Calcifications projecting over the right
iliac wing likely represent injection granulomas.  Fecal material is noted
within the distal colon.

IMPRESSION:  Nonspecific bowel gas pattern.  Nasogastric tube tip within the
stomach, however, side port is likely above the GE junction and should be
advanced.  No free intraperitoneal air.  A CT of the abdomen can be obtained
for further evaluation if there is continued concern for obstruction.
